{{smaller block|<poem>This very sword
Of mine slew more than any ''twain'' besides.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All is over — all is done,
''Twain'' of yesterday are one!</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The New Wife and the Old.}}}}

'''In twain''' (formerly also '''on twain'''), in or into two parts; asunder.
{{smaller block|With that stroke he brake his sheld ''on twayn.''
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2632.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now Death has come intill his bower,
And split his heart ''in twain.''</poem>
{{right|''Bonny Bee-Ho’m'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 58).}}}}

'''twain†''' (twān), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''twaynen''; < ''twain'', ''a.'' Cf. ''twin''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.''] To part in twain; divide; sunder.
{{smaller block|We in twynne wern towen & ''twayned.''
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), i. 251.}}}}
{{smaller block|It were great sin true love to ''twain''!
{{right|''Clerk Saunders'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 48).}}}}

'''twain-cloud''' (twān′kloud), ''n.'' In ''meteor.'', same as ''cumulo-stratus.'' See ''cloud''<sup>1</sup>, 1.

'''twaite<sup>1</sup>''' (twāt), ''n.'' An obsolete or dialectal variant of ''thwaite''<sup>1</sup>. ''Coke'', Instit., iv. b. (''Blount'', Glossographia, 1670.)

'''twaite<sup>2</sup>''' (twāt), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''tweat''; also, appar. by error, ''thwaite''; origin not ascertained.] A kind of shad, ''Alosa finta.'' Also ''twaite-shad.''
{{smaller block|<poem>The peel, the ''tweat'', the bottling, and the rest,
With many more, that in the deep doth lie.</poem>
{{right|''J. Dennys'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 175).}}}}

'''twal, twall''' (twäl), ''a.'' Scotch forms of ''twelve.''

'''twa-lofted''' (twä′lôf″ted), ''a.'' Having two lofts or stories. [Scotch.]

{{smaller block|<poem>Loud, on the heath, a ''twangle'' rush’d,
That rung out Supper, grand and big,
From the crack’d bell of Blarneygig.</poem>
{{right|''Colman'', Poetical Vagaries, p. 111. (''Davies.'')}}}}

¶
'''twangler''' (twang′glėr), ''n.'' One who twangles or twangs.

{{smaller block|Beaters of drums and ''twanglers'' of the wire.
{{right|''Library Mag.'', III. 773.}}}}

'''twank''' (twangk), ''v. i.'' [A var. of ''twang''<sup>1</sup>, implying a more abrupt sound.] To emit a sharp twang.

{{smaller block|A freeman of London has the privilege of disturbing a whole street, for an hour together, with the ''twanking'' of a brass kettle or a frying-pan. ''Addison'', Spectator, No. 251.}}

'''twank''' (twangk), ''n.'' [< ''twank, v.''] A sharp twang. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''twankay''' (twang′kā), ''n.'' [< Chinese ''t‘un-k‘i'', a rivulet near Yen-chow fu, in the west of the province of Chě-kiang, where this kind of tea is grown.] A brand of green tea grown and prepared in the western part of the province of Chě-kiang, China.

'''’twas''' (twoz). A contraction of ''it was''.

{{smaller block|Farewell, you mad rascals. To horse, come. ’''Twas'' well done, ’''twas'' well done.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iv. 4.}}}}

'''twat''' (twot), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] The female pudendum. ''Fletcher'', Poems, p. 104. (''Halliwell.'') [Vulgar.]

{{smaller block|''Twat.'' Pudendum muliebre. {{right|''Bailey'', 1727.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|tuzzy|6548|twat}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''tuzzy''' (tuz′i), ''n.''; pl. ''tuzzies'' (-iz). [Formerly also ''tussy''; dim. of ''tuzz''; cf. ''tuzzimuzzy''.] '''1.''' A tuft or bunch of hair. See the quotation. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|A ball of horsehair, such as is used by copper plate printers to assist in freeing their hands from ink (they call it a ''tuzzy'').
{{right|''Sci. Amer.'', N. S., LXII. 131.}}}}
Hence—'''2.''' A cluster or bunch of objects, as flowers; a bouquet. [Provincial.]
{{smaller block|A girdle of flowers and ''tussies'' of all fruits, intertyed and following together.
{{right|''Donne'', Hist. Septuagint (ed. 1633), p. 49. (''Richardson.'')}}}}

'''twa''' (twä or twȧ), ''a.'' An obsolete or Scotch form of ''two''.

'''Twaddell''' (twod′l), ''n.'' [Named after its inventor.] A hydrometer graduated so that each division represents the same change of density. {{smaller|It is used for densities greater than that of water, and the excess above unity is found by multiplying by 5 and dividing by 1,000 — that is, 200 divisions of the scale represent unity. Sometimes spelled ''Twaddle''.}}
{{smaller block|A ''Twaddle'' instrument constructed for liquids.
{{right|''O’Neill'', Dyeing and Calico Printing, p. 63.}}}}

'''twaddle''' (twod′l), ''v. i.''; pret. and pp. ''twaddled'', ppr. ''twaddling''. [A var. of ''twattle''.] To babble; gabble; prate; especially, to keep up a foolish, prosy chatter.
{{smaller block|Harry Warrington is green Telemachus, who, be sure, was very unlike the soft youth in the good Bishop of Cambray’s ''twaddling'' story.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Virginians, xviii.}}
To be sure, Cicero used to ''twaddle'' about Greek literature and philosophy, much as people do about ancient art now-a-days.
{{right|''Lowell'', Fireside Travels, p. 155.}}}}

'''twaddle''' (twod′l), ''n.'' [< ''twaddle, v.''] '''1.''' A twaddler.

{{smaller block|The fashionable words or favourite expressions of the day, . . . being superseded by new ones, vanish without leaving a trace behind. Such were the late fashionable words, a bore and a ''twaddle'', among the great vulgar.
{{right|''Grose'', Class. Dict. of Vulgar Tongue (ed. 1788), Pref., p. ix.}}
The devil take the ''twaddle!'' . . . I must tip him the cold shoulder, or he will be pestering me eternally.
{{right|''Scott'', St. Ronan’s Well, xxx.}}}}
'''2.''' Idle, senseless talk; gabble; prosy nonsense.
{{smaller block|He [Fielding] couldn’t do otherwise than laugh at the puny cockney bookseller [Richardson], pouring out endless volumes of sentimental ''twaddle''.
{{right|''Thackeray'', Hogarth, Smollett, and Fielding.}}}}
'''3.''' Perplexity; confusion. ''Grose'', Dict. of Vulgar Tongue. ='''Syn. 2.''' ''Chatter, Jargon'', etc. See ''prattle, n.''

'''twaddler''' (twod′lėr), ''n.'' [< ''twaddle'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] One who twaddles; a babbler; a prater.

{{smaller block|The cardinals appeared a wretched set of old ''twaddlers'', all but about three in extreme decrepitude.
{{right|''Greville'', Memoirs, April 4, 1830.}}}}

'''twaddling''' (twod′ling), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''twaddle, v.''] The act of one who twaddles; silly, empty talk; twaddle.

'''twaddly''' (twod′li), ''a.'' [< ''twaddle'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Consisting of twaddle; twaddling.

{{smaller block|It is rather an offensive word to use, especially considering the greatness of the writers who have treated the subject [old age]; but their lucubrations seem to me to be ''twaddly''.
{{right|''Helps.''}}}}

'''twae''' (twā), ''a.'' and ''n.'' A Scotch form of ''two''.

'''twagger†''' (twag′ėr), ''n.'' [Cf. ''twigger''.] A fat lamb.

<poem>And I have brought a ''twagger'' for the nones,</poem>
<poem>A bunting lamb; nay, pray, you feel no bones:
Believe me now, my cunning much I miss
If ever Pan felt fatter lamb than this.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Peele'', Arraignment of Paris, i. 1.}}}}

'''twain''' (twān), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''twayn'', ''twayne'', ''twein'', ''twey'', ''tweyn'', ''tweyne'', ''twaien'', ''twegen'', < AS. ''twēgen'' (= OS. OFries. ''twēne'' = D. ''twee'' = MLG. ''twēne'', ''tweine'', LG. ''twēne'' = OHG. ''zwēnē'', MHG. ''zwēne'', G. (obs.) ''zween'' = Dan. ''tvende'' = Sw. ''tvenné'' = Goth. ''twaihnai''), two; the masc. form of ''two'': see ''two''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Two. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|He . . . bad Bette kut a bow other ''tweyne''.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 32.}}
<poem>By than the yere was all agone
He had no man but ''twayne''.</poem>
{{right|''Lytell Geste of Robyn Hode'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 120).}}
<poem>Riding at noon, a day or ''twain'' before,
Across the forest call’d of Dean.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Pelleas and Ettarre.}}}}

'''To be twain''', {{smaller|to be two different persons or things; hence, to be separate or sundered.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Reason and I, you must conceive, ''are twain'';
’Tis nine years now since first I lost my wit.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Idea, ix.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' Two units, occurring or regarded either singly or separate; a couple; a pair. [Obsolete or archaic.]
{{smaller block|A man . . . shall cleave to his wife; and they ''twain'' shall be one flesh. . . . They are no more ''twain'' but one flesh.
{{right|Mat. xix. 5, 6.}}
<poem>Go with me
To bless this ''twain'', that they may prosperous be.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 104.}} <poem>This very sword
Of mine slew more than any ''twain'' besides.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All is over — all is done,
''Twain'' of yesterday are one!</poem>
{{right|''Whittier'', The New Wife and the Old.}}}}

'''In twain''' (formerly also '''on twain'''), in or into two parts; asunder.
{{smaller block|With that stroke he brake his sheld ''on twayn.''
{{right|''Generydes'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2632.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Now Death has come intill his bower,
And split his heart ''in twain.''</poem>
{{right|''Bonny Bee-Ho’m'' (Child’s Ballads, III. 58).}}}}

{{smaller block|We in twynne wern towen & ''twayned.''
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), i. 251.}}}}
{{smaller block|It were great sin true love to ''twain''!
{{right|''Clerk Saunders'' (Child’s Ballads, II. 48).}}}}

'''twain-cloud''' (twān′kloud), ''n.'' In ''meteor.'', same as ''cumulo-stratus.'' See ''cloud''<sup>1</sup>, 1.

'''twaite<sup>1</sup>''' (twāt), ''n.'' An obsolete or dialectal variant of ''thwaite''<sup>1</sup>. ''Coke'', Instit., iv. b. (''Blount'', Glossographia, 1670.)

'''twaite<sup>2</sup>''' (twāt), ''n.'' [Formerly also ''tweat''; also, appar. by error, ''thwaite''; origin not ascertained.] A kind of shad, ''Alosa finta.'' Also ''twaite-shad.''
{{smaller block|<poem>The peel, the ''tweat'', the bottling, and the rest,
With many more, that in the deep doth lie.</poem>
{{right|''J. Dennys'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 175).}}}}

'''twal, twall''' (twäl), ''a.'' Scotch forms of ''twelve.''

'''twa-lofted''' (twä′lôf″ted), ''a.'' Having two lofts or stories. [Scotch.] {{smaller block|Folks are far frae respecting me as they wad do if I lived in a ''twa-lofted'' sclated house.
{{right|''Scott'', Bride of Lammermoor, xxiv.}}}}

'''twalpennies''' (twal′pen″iz), ''n. pl.'' Twelvepence in the old Scottish currency, equal to one penny sterling.
{{smaller block|Saunders, in addition to the customary ''twalpennies'' on the postage, had a dram for his pains.
{{right|''Galt'', Ayrshire Legatees, ii.}}}}

'''twan†.''' An obsolete preterit of ''twine''<sup>1</sup>.

'''twang'''<sup>1</sup> (twang), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. also ''twangue;'' ult. imitative; cf. ''tang'' and ''ting''.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To give out a sharp, metallic ring, as the string of a musical instrument, a bow, etc., when plucked and suddenly set free: said also of other instruments which make a similar sound.
{{smaller block|To ''Twangue'', resonare.
{{right|''Levins'', Manip. Vocab. (E. E. T. S.), p. 23.}}
<poem>Yet, shooting upward, sends his shaft, to show
An archer’s art, and boasts his ''twanging'' bow.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, v. 688.}}
Hark! ’tis the ''twanging'' horn o’er yonder bridge.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 1.}}
''Twang'' out, my fiddle: {{right|''Tennyson'', Amphion.}}}}
'''2.''' To make music on a stringed instrument that is played by plucking or snapping; cause a sharp ringing sound like that of a harp or bowstring: as, to ''twang'' on a jews’-harp.
{{smaller block|When the harper ''twangeth'' or singeth a song, all the companie must be whist.
{{right|''Stanihurst'', Descrip. of Ireland, viii. (Holinshed’s Chron., I.).}}}}
'''3.''' To have a nasal sound: said of the human voice; also, to speak with a nasal twang: said of persons.
{{smaller block|Every accent ''twanged''.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''4†.''' To shoot with a bow; make a shot; hence, figuratively, to surmise; guess.
{{smaller block|''Hor.'' These be black slaves; Romans, take heed of these.
''Tuc.'' Thou ''twang’st'' right, little Horace: they be indeed a couple of chap-fallen curs.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Poetaster, v. 1.}}}}
'''To go off twanging†''', to go well; go swimmingly.
{{smaller block|<poem>An old fool, to be gull’d thus! had he died, . . .
It had ''gone off twanging''.</poem>
{{right|''Massinger'', Roman Actor, ii. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to sound with a short sharp ring; set in quick, resounding vibration, as the tense string of a bow or a musical instrument that is played by plucking: said less frequently of wind-instruments.
{{smaller block|The Fleet in View, he ''twang’d'' his deadly Bow.
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, i. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|The old original post, with the stamp in the corner, representing a post-boy riding for life and ''twanging'' his horn.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Cranford, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|A black-haired girl . . . ''twangs'' a stringed instrument with taper fingers.
{{right|''Harper’s Mag.'', LXXIX. 492.}}}}
'''2.''' To sound forth by means of a twanging instrument.
{{smaller block|The trumpeter strutted up and down the ramparts ''twanging'' defiance to the whole Yankee race, as does a modern editor to all the principalities and powers on the other side of the Atlantic.
{{right|''Irving'', Knickerbocker, p. 225.}}}} '''3.''' To utter with a short, sharp, or nasal sound; specifically, to pronounce with a nasal twang.
{{smaller block|A terrible oath, with a swaggering accent sharply ''twanged'' off.
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4. 198.}}
The cicerone ''twangs'' his moral, and the blue sky shines calmly over the ruin. ''Thackeray'', Congreve and Addison.}}

'''twang<sup>1</sup>''' (twang), ''n.'' [< ''twang''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] '''1.''' The sound of a tense string set in sudden sharp vibration by plucking; hence, any sharp, ringing musical sound.
{{smaller block|If Cynthia hear the ''twang'' of my bow, she’ll go near to whip me with the string.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Cynthia’s Revels, v. 3.}}
<poem>The sharp clear ''twang'' of the golden chords
Runs up the ridged sea. ''Tennyson'', Sea Fairies.</poem>}}
'''2.''' A sharp, ringing nasal tone, especially of the human voice.
{{smaller block|I like your southern accent: it is so pure, so soft. It has no rugged burr, no nasal ''twang'', such as almost every one’s voice here in the north has.
{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Shirley, xxv.}}
No signs of life occurred near him, but occasionally the melancholy chirp of a cricket, or perhaps the guttural ''twang'' of a bull-frog from a neighboring marsh.
{{right|''Irving'', Sketch-Book, p. 446.}}}}

'''twang<sup>1</sup>''' (twang), ''interj.'' or ''adv.'' [An elliptical use of ''twang''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.''] An exclamation or sound imitative of the twang of a bowstring, harpstring, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>It made John sing, to hear the gold ring,
Which against the walls cryed ''twang''.</poem>
{{right|''Little John and the Four Beggars'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 327).}}
<poem>There ’s one, the best in all my Quiver,
''Twang!'' thro’ his very Heart and Liver.</poem>
{{right|''Prior'', Mercury and Cupid.}}}}

'''twang<sup>2</sup>†''' (twang), ''n.'' [A var. of ''tang''<sup>2</sup>.] A sharp taste; a disagreeable after-taste or flavor left in the mouth; a tang; a flavor. [Prov. Eng.]
{{smaller block|Such were my reflections; . . . it seems, from the illustration, they already began to have a ''twang'' of commerce in them. {{right|''Scott'', Rob Roy, xviii.}}
Hot, bilious, with a confounded ''twang'' in his mouth, and a cracking pain in his head, he stood one moment and snuffed in the salt sea breeze. {{right|''Disraeli'', Young Duke, iv. 6.}}}}

'''twang<sup>3</sup>''' (twang), ''n.'' [Prob. < ''twang''<sup>1</sup>, with sense imported from ''twinge''.] A sharp pull; a sudden pang, a twinge. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My curse upon thy venom’d stang,
That shoots my tortur’d gums alang,
An’ through my lugs gi’es mony a ''twang''.</poem>{{right|''Burns'', Address to the Toothache.}}}}

'''twangle''' (twang′gl), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''twangled'', ppr. ''twangling''. [Freq. of ''twang''<sup>1</sup>.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To twang lightly or frequently: said either of an instrument or of its player.
{{smaller block|<poem>She did call me rascal fiddler
And ''twangling'' Jack. ''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1. 159.</poem>
<poem>Sometimes a thousand ''twangling'' instruments
Will hum about mine ears, and sometimes voices.</poem>{{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iii. 2. 146.}}
<poem>“Ay, fool,” said Tristram, “but ’tis eating dry
To dance without a catch, a roundelay
To dance to.” Then he ''twangled'' on his harp.</poem>{{right|''Tennyson'', Last Tournament.}}}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To cause to twangle.
{{smaller block|The young Andrea bears up gayly, however; ''twangles'' his guitar. {{right|''Thackeray'', Shabby Genteel Story, ii.}}}}

'''twangle†''' (twang′gl), ''n.'' [< ''twangle'', ''v.''] A twangling sound; a twang or clang.
<poem>Loud, on the heath, a ''twangle'' rush’d,
That rung out Supper, grand and big,
From the crack’d bell of Blarneygig.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Colman'', Poetical Vagaries, p. 111. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''twangler''' (twang′glėr), ''n.'' One who twangles or twangs.

{{smaller block|Beaters of drums and ''twanglers'' of the wire.
{{right|''Library Mag.'', III. 773.}}}}

'''twank''' (twangk), ''v. i.'' [A var. of ''twang''<sup>1</sup>, implying a more abrupt sound.] To emit a sharp twang.

{{smaller block|A freeman of London has the privilege of disturbing a whole street, for an hour together, with the ''twanking'' of a brass kettle or a frying-pan. ''Addison'', Spectator, No. 251.}}

'''twank''' (twangk), ''n.'' [< ''twank, v.''] A sharp twang. ''Imp. Dict.''

'''twankay''' (twang′kā), ''n.'' [< Chinese ''t‘un-k‘i'', a rivulet near Yen-chow fu, in the west of the province of Chě-kiang, where this kind of tea is grown.] A brand of green tea grown and prepared in the western part of the province of Chě-kiang, China.

'''’twas''' (twoz). A contraction of ''it was''.

{{smaller block|Farewell, you mad rascals. To horse, come. ’''Twas'' well done, ’''twas'' well done.
{{right|''Dekker and Webster'', Northward Ho, iv. 4.}}}}

'''twat''' (twot), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] The female pudendum. ''Fletcher'', Poems, p. 104. (''Halliwell.'') [Vulgar.]

{{smaller block|''Twat.'' Pudendum muliebre. {{right|''Bailey'', 1727.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
